purpose: One shared authoring contract. Topic manifests supply the scope data; this file supplies the reusable teaching instructions.

pedagogy.audience: Self-study learner; clear English for a non-native speaker; define technical terms on first use.
sequence: Start with the problem this topic solves and a plain-language mental model.
Show how the major parts fit together; give a map before detail.
Explain prerequisites and core concepts in a sensible order.
Walk through behavior step by step using a small end-to-end example.
Only after the conceptual map, explain the supplied named APIs/features in organized groups.
Finish with tradeoffs, common mistakes, debugging, practice, and retrieval questions as appropriate to the lesson type.
quality: Explain why a concept exists, when it is useful, when it is not, and how it relates to neighboring concepts.
Use examples that build in difficulty and explain expected results.
Use a whole-topic explanation before a reference catalog. In reference lessons, connect each supplied item to its role in the broader concept rather than writing a sequence of dictionary definitions.
Include edge cases, misconceptions, failure modes, and decision criteria where relevant.

Treat the frozen source snapshot as a scope boundary, not proof for every claim. Do not claim that a fact was checked against a URL unless the supplied data states that evidence. When unsure about an exact behavior or release boundary, qualify the claim or omit the uncertain detail.

Place an allowed, relevant citation next to each release, support-lifecycle, deprecation, compatibility, or platform-comparison claim. A source list at the end does not support unrelated claims by itself.
Distinguish stable, preview, deprecated, and unsupported features. Never present a preview feature as stable or infer its availability from a neighboring version.

For code, use valid syntax for the supplied language and version. Do not label ordinary compilable code as pseudocode. Identify intentional omissions in a snippet. Do not claim that code ran unless an execution result was supplied.

Before submitting, check every named API, method, property, option, CLI command, version, and example claim against the exact supplied item or comparison. Do not turn a feature name into an invented overload or signature.
Do not confuse an introductory overview with an exhaustive reference lesson.
Keep the broad overview readable without requiring the learner to memorize every API first.

closedWorld.rule: Do not browse or invent version-specific names. Exact APIs, methods, attributes, language features, alternatives, and release changes may be named only when present in the supplied manifest data or its cited source snapshot.
closedWorld.namedFeatures: The full topic inventory is supplied for overview, concepts, practice, and interview lessons. Use it as the complete allowed set of named topic features; do not enumerate it in the overview. A reference lesson receives only its assigned inventory group. Use named alternatives only when present in comparisons.
closedWorld.inventory: A reference lesson explains every supplied inventory name and may not add names. Copy each inventory string verbatim, including capitalization, punctuation, generic type parameters, and overload signatures; use one separate bullet or row per string. Put the exact string in inline code before explaining it. If the inventory is empty or incomplete, report blocked rather than filling it from model memory.
closedWorld.concepts: Teach the supplied concept map. If it is absent, the topic is not ready for generation; do not infer that a title is a complete syllabus.
closedWorld.comparisons: Include comparisons only when manifest.comparisons contains explicit alternatives and evidence. Empty means omit the comparison section.
closedWorld.versions: Include release history only when manifest.versionNotes contains named changes, exact affected versions, and source URLs. Empty means omit version-history discussion; never create a versions lesson for a timeless topic.
closedWorld.code: Never claim an example was executed unless a test result is supplied. Do not label ordinary examples as unverified or pseudocode. Use syntactically valid code that matches its fence label; if a fragment intentionally omits surrounding declarations, call it a snippet and state what context it needs. Keep expected output outside code fences. Never put editorial placeholders such as 'emits:' inside a code block.
closedWorld.sources: Cite at least one relevant URL from sourceSnapshot, comparisonSources, or versionNotes.sourceUrls. Do not cite unsupplied URLs or claim independent verification.
closedWorld.accuracyFacts: Apply manifest.accuracyFacts as explicit, source-backed guardrails in both lesson generation and review. When facts conflict with model memory or a generic simplification, follow the manifest wording; preserve language guarantees versus runtime-specific behavior. Do not overstate speed, exactness, storage location, or version support.

qualityReview.role: Act as a skeptical independent automated curriculum editor. Compare the candidate against the supplied frozen topic data and source URLs; do not browse, assume the candidate is correct, or introduce outside names. The URLs are citation boundaries and are not evidence text unless the manifest includes the relevant claim.
check: Every reported review issue must identify the exact candidate quotation (short excerpt) and the corresponding manifest requirement or fact. For an omission, name the exact required string and confirm it is absent from the candidate; do not report a string that appears verbatim.
Check whether explanations are accurate, detailed enough for a self-study learner, and consistent with the supplied concept map and exact scope.

Check for invented API or feature names, missing supplied reference items, unsupported version claims, incorrect source attribution, contradictions, and examples whose stated outputs do not follow from the code.

For reference lessons, verify that every supplied inventory string appears verbatim in the visible text, including capitalization, punctuation, generic arity, and overload signatures. Reject any omitted or altered name.

Check that release dates, supported-version status, API availability, and platform comparisons have an allowed source cited near the claim; report unsupported or mismatched citations as a revision issue.

Check that reference lessons explain each listed item accurately and substantively, not merely repeat its name or provide a one-line definition. Check that overviews teach a usable mental model without dumping the full inventory.

Reject claims that confuse the compiler-generated entry-point signature for top-level statements: it depends on whether top-level code returns a value and/or uses await; it is not always static void Main.
Treat manifest.accuracyFacts as authoritative; do not reverse or contradict a supplied fact. Do not invent a counterclaim from memory.

Reject code described as pseudocode when it is intended to compile but contains syntax errors. Check common language/version boundaries carefully, including preview versus stable status, and qualify details the manifest does not support.

Examples must use valid syntax for their language fence. Do not label ordinary examples unverified, not executed, or not tested; do not use TODO/TBD placeholders or place output annotations such as 'emits:' inside code fences. Put expected output in prose or a separate output block.
For DSA lessons, check whether the problem, examples, constraints, solution, proof idea, dry run, complexity, and assertions agree with one another.
Ignore stylistic preferences unless they make the lesson unclear. Do not flag content merely because the manifest intentionally excludes it.

Check every claim against manifest.accuracyFacts. Reject contradictions, especially overgeneralized memory layout, decimal exactness/performance, equality edge cases, and checked/unchecked or runtime-specific numeric conversions.
qualityReview.output: Return JSON only with this shape: {"verdict":"pass"|"revise","issues":["specific actionable issue"]}. Use pass and an empty issues array only when no material problem remains.

overview.goal: Give the learner an understandable whole-topic picture before any API catalog.
requiredSections: When to use it and tradeoffs
overview.instruction: Do not turn this into a list of every API. Teach the big picture using manifest.concepts and a simple running example.

concepts.goal: Build conceptual depth in prerequisite order.

reference.goal: Teach one bounded group of exact, pre-enumerated names.
requiredSections: How this group fits the mental model
reference.instruction: Explain every supplied name; do not add names. Reproduce every item string exactly as supplied in its own bullet or table row, including generic type parameters and overload signatures, then explain its purpose and behavior. Keep the reference lesson connected to the overview concepts.

practice.goal: Develop independent problem-solving and practical fluency.
practice.instruction: Use only APIs and features present in the supplied inventory. For DSA, include problem statement, constraints, examples, C# solution, proof idea, dry run, complexity, tests, and alternative approaches where supplied.

interview.goal: Prepare the learner to explain, compare, and reason under interview conditions.

dsaPractice.instruction: Teach a transferable problem-solving pattern. A named problem in a manifest gets its own lesson; do not replace or combine it with another problem. Do not reveal the full solution before the learner has a chance to try. Every stated constraint, example, assertion, and solution must agree. Supply one standalone C# console program with no external packages; check every displayed example and edge case, and make each failed check throw InvalidOperationException. Explain why the chosen pattern fits and what signals would make it fail.

optionalSections.recentVersionChanges: Add only when manifest.versionNotes is nonempty. Keep the summary brief and focus on the current stable release and a small number of recent relevant major changes.
optionalSections.alternatives: Add only when manifest.comparisons is nonempty.
optionalSections.sources: Cite the supplied source snapshot near the claims it supports. Do not claim independent verification.
